objectives: Identify peptide bonds and synthesis carbon sources
Distinguish phosphate linkages and reaction energetics

cards.rule: An alpha amino acid has amino and carboxyl groups attached to the same alpha carbon. At many near-neutral pH conditions, simple amino acids predominantly form zwitterions. Side chains add nonpolar, aromatic, polar, acidic, or basic behavior. Glycine has no stereocenter; most proteinogenic L amino acids are S, with cysteine the familiar R exception. Amino acids are amphoteric: an acidic carboxyl group can donate H+ and a basic amino group can accept H+; side chains may add further ionizable sites.
cards.cue: Low pH adds protons; high pH removes them. Net charge is the sum of all ionized groups.
cards.trap: A zwitterion has formal charges despite net zero charge. The pI is the pH of average net zero charge; for ionizable side chains, average the two pKa values bracketing the neutral species, not automatically the terminal pKa pair.
cards.app: Aliphatic side chains such as Ala, Val, Leu, and Ile are nonpolar; Ser and Thr have polar OH groups; Asn and Gln have polar amides. Asp/Glu are usually negatively charged near neutral pH; Lys/Arg usually positive. Histidine protonation is strongly pH- and environment-dependent. Aromatic does not always mean purely nonpolar: Tyr has a phenolic OH. At pH below pI a protein tends positive; above pI it tends negative. Methionine has a largely nonpolar thioether side chain; cysteine has a polar thiol and can form disulfides on oxidation. Proline has a cyclic side chain bonded to its nitrogen (a secondary amine in the free amino acid); phenylalanine and tryptophan are commonly grouped as nonpolar aromatic amino acids, although tryptophan has an indole N–H donor.

steps.text: The nitrogen bears positive charge and the carboxylate bears negative charge. Its alpha carbon also has methyl and H. This connectivity drawing leaves stereochemistry unspecified.

rule.title: Amino Acid Zwitterions, Titration Curves & Isoelectric Point (pI) Formulas
rule.formula: Neutral R: pI = ½(pKa_COOH + pKa_NH3+)   |   Acidic (Asp/Glu): pI = ½(pKa_COOH + pKa_R)   |   Basic (Lys/Arg/His): pI = ½(pKa_R + pKa_NH3+)

items.label: Why Never Average All 3 pKa Values!
items.text: Always find the neutral Zwitterion species (net charge = 0) first, then average ONLY the two pKa steps that immediately create and destroy that 0-charge form!

items.label: Key Side-Chain pKa Values to Memorize
items.text: Asp (~3.7), Glu (~4.3), His (~6.0, near physiological pH!), Cys (~8.3), Tyr (~10.1), Lys (~10.5), Arg (~12.5).

comparison: Fully protonated (+1 or +2 if basic R)
Fully deprotonated (−1 or −2 if acidic R)

cue.title: Instant Amino Acid Charge & Isoelectric Point (pI) Calculator
cue.prompt: Which amino acid class are you calculating pI or charge for at pH 7.4?

items.label: Nonpolar / Uncharged Polar (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Ser, Thr, Asn, Gln)
items.outcome: pI ≈ ½(2.2 + 9.5) ≈ 5.8–6.0 | Net Charge at pH 7.4 = 0
items.text: Only two ionizable groups exist: α-COO⁻ (−1) and α-NH₃⁺ (+1) cancel to zero net charge at pH 7.4.

items.label: Acidic Side Chains: Aspartate (D) & Glutamate (E)
items.outcome: pI = ½(pKa1_αCOOH + pKa2_R) ≈ 3.0 | Net Charge at pH 7.4 = −1
items.text: Neutral zwitterion sits between the two acidic deprotonations (around pH 3); at pH 7.4 both carboxylates are −1 plus one +1 α-NH₃⁺ = −1 net.

items.label: Basic Side Chains: Lysine (K), Arginine (R) & Histidine (H)
items.outcome: pI = ½(pKa2_R + pKa3_αNH3+) ≈ 9.7–10.8 (His ≈ 7.6) | Charge at pH 7.4: Lys/Arg = +1, His ≈ 0
items.text: Neutral zwitterion requires deprotonating α-COOH (−1) AND one of the two ammonium groups (+1); average the two higher pKa values!

trap.title: Drawing Uncharged H₂N–CH(R)–COOH in Water or Averaging All 3 pKa Values for pI

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Averaging (2.0 + 3.9 + 9.8)/3 for Aspartate’s pI, or drawing an amino acid with neutral –NH₂ and neutral –COOH in the same molecule.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Because –COOH (pKa ~2) is a billion times more acidic than –NH₃⁺ (pKa ~9.5), –COOH ALWAYS loses its proton long before –NH₃⁺ does (forming the dipolar zwitterion)! Average only the 2 pKas flanking the 0-charge species.

app.title: Gel Electrophoresis Migration, Ion-Exchange Chromatography & Histidine Buffering

items.label: Native Gel Electrophoresis / Isoelectric Focusing
items.outcome: pH > pI → Negative Charge (Moves to Anode +)
items.text: If buffer pH > pI, the amino acid or protein is deprotonated (net negative); if pH < pI, it is protonated (net positive); at pH = pI, migration stops!

items.label: Histidine Imidazole Ring (pKa ~6.0)
items.outcome: General Acid–Base Catalyst at pH 7.4
items.text: Because pKa ~6.0 is close to physiological pH 7.4, Histidine exists in both protonated (+1) and neutral (0) forms at room temperature—ideal for shuttling H⁺ in enzymes!

items.label: Aromatic UV Absorbance at 280 nm
items.outcome: Trp (W) > Tyr (Y) ≫ Phe (F)
items.text: Conjugated indole (Trp) and phenol (Tyr) rings absorb UV light at 280 nm, enabling rapid protein concentration measurement (Beer-Lambert law A = εcl).

cards.rule: A peptide bond joins one residue’s carbonyl carbon to the next residue’s nitrogen. Resonance makes the peptide group approximately planar with restricted C–N rotation. Sequence is conventionally read N-terminus → C-terminus. Primary sequence supports secondary structures, tertiary folding, and sometimes quaternary assembly. Net peptide formation is a condensation/dehydration, eliminating water from amino and carboxyl groups in formal bookkeeping. Activation enables synthesis; hydrolysis consumes water to cleave the amide, with enzymes or suitable strong acid/base and often heat. Basic cleavage is base-promoted and gives carboxylate, not necessarily a neutral acid before workup.
cards.cue: N to C is the reading direction. Peptide C–N is the restricted bond; adjacent backbone single bonds supply much of the flexibility.
cards.trap: A peptide bond is not a C–C bond between two alpha carbons. Peptide formation is thermodynamically and kinetically enabled by activation in cells; plain amino acids in water do not rapidly polymerize by themselves.
cards.app: Hydrogen bonding organizes alpha helices and beta sheets; hydrophobic effects and side-chain interactions help stabilize folded proteins.

steps.label: 1. Find the amide linkage
steps.text: The internal nitrogen is bonded directly to the preceding carbonyl carbon. The terminal amino and carboxyl groups remain available for ionization.

steps.label: 2. Trace the backbone
steps.text: Follow N–Cα–C(=O)–N–Cα–C(=O). The peptide C–N link is approximately planar because the N lone pair participates in resonance.

rule.title: Peptide Bond Resonance Planarity, N→C Convention & Protein Structure Levels (1°–4°)

items.label: Directional N-Terminus → C-Terminus Convention
items.text: Amide resonance gives partial C–N double-bond character and a nearly planar peptide group. Trans is usually favored; cis populations depend on the residue and environment.

items.label: Partial Double-Bond Character of the Peptide Bond
items.text: Resonance (O=C–NH ↔ ⁻O–C=NH⁺) gives the C–N bond ~40% π character (1.32 Å vs 1.47 Å), locking all 6 peptide-plane atoms in a rigid TRANS planar conformation (except ~6% cis before Proline).

items.label: Denaturation vs. Hydrolysis
items.text: Urea, guanidinium HCl, heat, or pH extremes disrupt noncovalent 2°/3°/4° interactions (and β-mercaptoethanol/DTT reduces Cys–S–S–Cys disulfides), leaving the covalent 1° peptide sequence completely intact!

comparison: Covalent peptide (amide) bonds; cleaved by 6M HCl/proteases
Backbone C=O···H–N H-bonds ONLY (Proline = helix breaker!)
Hydrophobic core, salt bridges, H-bonds, Cys–S–S–Cys disulfides

figure.caption: Locate the peptide C–N linkage and the termini. The drawing is not a measured three-dimensional geometry.

cue.title: Protease Cleavage Specificity & Protein Structure Disrupter Guide
cue.prompt: Which reagent or enzyme is acting on the protein?

items.label: Trypsin vs. Chymotrypsin vs. Cyanogen Bromide (CNBr)
items.outcome: Trypsin = C-side of Lys/Arg; Chymotrypsin = C-side of Phe/Tyr/Trp; CNBr = C-side of Met
items.text: Wait: Proline immediately after the target residue blocks trypsin/chymotrypsin cleavage! The final fragment with NO cleavage site at its C-end is the original C-terminus.

items.label: Urea / Heat vs. β-Mercaptoethanol (BME) / DTT
items.outcome: Urea Breaks H-Bonds (2°/3°); BME Reduces Disulfide Bridges (Cys–S–S–Cys → 2 Cys–SH)
items.text: In SDS-PAGE, non-reducing vs. reducing gels reveal whether subunits are linked by covalent disulfide bridges!

items.label: Proline & Glycine in α-Helices
items.outcome: Both Disrupt α-Helices ("Helix Breakers"), Found in β-Turns & Collagen!
items.text: Proline is a secondary amine (lacks a backbone N–H H-bond donor and has a rigid ring); Glycine is too conformationally flexible (high ΔS cost to fold).

trap.title: Thinking Denaturation Breaks Peptide Bonds or Saying Secondary Structure Uses Side-Chain H-Bonds

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Saying boiling an egg or adding 8M urea hydrolyzes peptide bonds, or saying α-helices are held together by R-group interactions.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Secondary structure (α-helix and β-sheet) is stabilized EXCLUSIVELY by BACKBONE amide C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds; side-chain R-group interactions define tertiary (3°) structure!

app.title: Insulin Disulfide Processing, Edman Degradation & SDS-PAGE Analysis

items.label: Reducing vs. Non-Reducing SDS-PAGE
items.outcome: 100 kDa Band Alone vs. 50 kDa Band + BME
items.text: If a 100 kDa protein drops to 50 kDa ONLY when β-mercaptoethanol is added, it is a homodimer linked by an interchain disulfide bond!

items.label: α-Helix Geometry (3.6 Residues/Turn)
items.outcome: C=O of Residue i H-Bonds to N–H of Residue (i + 4)
items.text: All side chains point outward from the helix cylinder; transmembrane α-helices require ~20 hydrophobic amino acids to span a lipid bilayer.

items.label: Sanger / Edman N-Terminal Sequencing
items.outcome: Labels & Cleaves the N-Terminal Residue (1° Structure)
items.text: Identifies the exact N-terminal amino acid without hydrolyzing the rest of the peptide chain.

lessons.label: Strecker and Gabriel amino-acid strategies
lessons.title: Strecker and Gabriel amino-acid strategies
lessons.tag: Track where the carboxyl carbon comes from

cards.rule: In the Strecker route, an aldehyde reacts through an imine/iminium stage with ammonia and cyanide to form an alpha-aminonitrile. Nitrile hydrolysis gives the carboxyl group. A Gabriel–malonic ester route installs protected nitrogen and an alkyl side chain, then hydrolyzes and decarboxylates to an alpha amino acid. One Strecker teaching reagent set uses NH4Cl/KCN, followed by aqueous acid and heat: imine/iminium formation, cyanide carbon addition, then nitrile hydrolysis. These are reaction-recognition details, not an experimental procedure.
cards.cue: Strecker: nitrile carbon becomes carboxyl carbon. Gabriel–malonate: alkylation builds the side chain; decarboxylation removes one carboxyl group. In the Gabriel–malonic ester variant, potassium phthalimide substitutes at the brominated carbon of diethyl bromomalonate. Deprotonation of the protected aminomalonate then enables carbon alkylation with a suitable alkyl halide by SN2. Hydrolysis/deprotection and decarboxylation give the amino acid; the phthalimide framework can leave as phthalic acid under acidic hydrolysis conditions. The electrophile must be compatible with SN2; tertiary halides do not serve as a universal choice.
cards.trap: Achiral starting materials and conditions usually give a racemic chiral amino-acid product; glycine is achiral. Ordinary Gabriel amine synthesis and the malonic-ester amino-acid variant are related but not identical.
cards.app: Laboratory racemic synthesis contrasts with enzyme-controlled production of stereochemically selected amino acids.

steps.label: 1. Aminonitrile intermediate
steps.text: The central carbon carries an amino group, methyl, H, and a nitrile carbon. This is the carbon skeleton leading to alanine on nitrile hydrolysis. Green tracks the nitrile-derived future carboxyl carbon, red the future alpha carbon, and orange the retained methyl side chain. The nitrile N is not retained in the amino acid.

steps.label: 2. Carbon bookkeeping
steps.text: The nitrile carbon becomes the amino acid’s carboxyl carbon. The original aldehyde carbon becomes its alpha carbon; the methyl side chain is retained. Protonation state then depends on pH.

steps.label: 3. Alternative protected route
steps.text: The phthalimide anion shown supplies protected nitrogen; its potassium counterion is omitted. N substitution on diethyl bromomalonate installs the protected amino group. Subsequent malonate carbon alkylation installs a side chain; hydrolysis/deprotection and decarboxylation then give an alpha amino acid. This reagent canvas is not the complete reaction sequence.

rule.title: Strecker & Amidomalonate / Gabriel Amino Acid Syntheses (Preventing Polyalkylation)

items.label: Why Direct Alkylation (NH₃ + RX) Fails for 1° Amines
items.text: Once RNH₂ forms, its inductive alkyl group makes it MORE nucleophilic than NH₃, causing rapid over-alkylation to R₂NH, R₃N, and R₄N⁺X⁻.

items.label: Strecker Synthesis (Aldehyde + NH₃ + HCN, then H₃O⁺/Δ)
items.text: Step 1: Aldehyde + NH₃ ⇌ Imine (RCH=NH). Step 2: CN⁻ attacks imine → α-aminonitrile (RCH(NH₂)CN). Step 3: Acid hydrolysis converts –CN to –COOH!

items.label: Gabriel Phthalimide + Malonic Ester Synthesis
items.text: Potassium phthalimide acts as a bulky, masked NH₂⁻ nucleophile that can only undergo ONE SN2 reaction on α-bromomalonic ester, followed by α-alkylation (R–X), ester/imide hydrolysis, and thermal decarboxylation (−CO₂).

chips: Strecker: Aldehyde + NH₃ + HCN → α-Aminonitrile → (±)-Amino Acid
comparison: Gives messy mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines + 4° ammonium salt
Imine + CN⁻ → α-aminonitrile → hydrolyzed to racemic (±)-amino acid

figure.caption: Nitrile-carbon tracking through hydrolysis. Product is drawn as a zwitterion after appropriate workup; not a balanced equation.

cue.title: Tracing Every Atom in Strecker vs. Gabriel-Malonate Amino Acid Synthesis
cue.prompt: Where does each piece of the synthesized α-amino acid come from?

items.label: Strecker Synthesis: Aldehyde R–CHO + NH₃ + KCN
items.outcome: R–CH comes from Aldehyde; –NH₃⁺ from NH₃; –COOH from Cyanide (CN⁻)!
items.text: Wait: The aldehyde carbonyl carbon becomes the α-CARBON (C2) of the amino acid, while the cyanide carbon becomes the C1 CARBOXYLIC ACID!

items.label: Gabriel Malonic Ester Synthesis + R–Br
items.outcome: Glycine Backbone from Bromomalonate; Side Chain R from R–Br!
items.text: Deprotonating the α-carbon of N-phthalimidomalonic ester with NaOEt followed by SN2 with R–Br installs the side chain R, and H₃O⁺/Δ cleaves the esters + decarboxylates one –COOH.

items.label: What Is the Stereochemistry of Uncatalyzed Strecker or Gabriel Products?
items.outcome: Achiral conditions: racemic chiral product; glycine is achiral
items.text: Achiral starting materials produce a planar imine (Strecker) or planar enol during decarboxylation (Gabriel), giving 0% ee unless resolved!

trap.title: Thinking the Aldehyde Carbon Becomes the –COOH Group in the Strecker Synthesis

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Assuming the C=O carbon of R–CHO becomes the carboxylic acid in a Strecker synthesis, or forgetting the +1 carbon added by CN⁻.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: In the Strecker synthesis, the aldehyde carbon becomes the α-carbon (CH–R), and the cyanide (–C≡N) carbon is hydrolyzed into the –COOH group (total carbons = Aldehyde C + 1)!

app.title: Prebiotic Amino Acid Origins, Azide Reduction & Reductive Amination of α-Keto Acids

items.label: Biological Transamination vs. Lab Strecker
items.outcome: α-Keto Acid + Glu (PLP) → Pure L-Amino Acid
items.text: Whereas Strecker makes racemic (±)-amino acids from an aldehyde + HCN, cells convert α-keto acids (pyruvate → L-alanine) stereospecifically via PLP transaminases!

items.label: Hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) Phthalimide Cleavage
items.outcome: Releases Free 1° Amine Under Mild Conditions
items.text: Hydrazine attacks both imide carbonyls of the Gabriel adduct to form a stable cyclic phthalhydrazide byproduct plus the clean 1° amine.

items.label: Protecting Groups in Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis
items.outcome: Boc (Cleaved by TFA Acid) & Fmoc (Cleaved by Piperidine Base)
items.text: Synthesizes peptides C → N on resin beads using N-protected amino acids + DCC/EDC coupling to prevent self-polymerization.

cards.rule: A phosphate ester contains P–O–C; a phosphodiester has two such ester links. A phosphoanhydride contains P–O–P. Phosphoric acid has successive dissociations, so charge depends on pH. Formal P=O Lewis drawings are bookkeeping models of delocalized bonding. Organic phosphate esters attach carbon groups through P–O–C. Inorganic orthophosphate (Pi) lacks such ester links and includes protonation states set by pH. Pyrophosphate (PPi) joins two phosphate units through P–O–P; its charge also depends on pH.
cards.cue: DNA/RNA backbone: phosphodiester. Between ATP phosphate groups: phosphoanhydride. Approximate aqueous phosphoric-acid pKa values are 2.1, 7.2 and 12.3; H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻ buffers near neutral pH. Temperature and ionic conditions shift the values. Useful buffering regions lie near each pKa, often within about one pH unit; capacity depends on concentration and component ratio. Three separated regions do not give uniformly effective buffering at all intervening pH values.
cards.trap: Breaking a bond requires energy. Favorable ATP hydrolysis reflects the overall free-energy difference between reactants and solvated products, including resonance, electrostatics, and solvation; energy is not released simply by breaking one bond.
cards.app: Phosphoryl transfer can couple reactions. Nucleic-acid synthesis releases pyrophosphate, whose subsequent hydrolysis can help favor polymerization.

steps.label: 1. Acidic phosphate
steps.text: The neutral phosphoric-acid representation has three OH groups. Sequential deprotonation gives different phosphate ions; this drawing is not the predominant form at every pH.

steps.label: 2. Phosphodiester model
steps.text: Dimethyl phosphate illustrates two P–O–C connections and a negative charge. The nucleic-acid backbone replaces the methyl groups with sugar-derived groups.

challenge.explanation: A is P, the central atom in the phosphate group.

rule.title: Phosphoric Acid Speciation (pKa 2.1, 7.2, 12.4), ATP Bioenergetics & Phosphodiester Stability

items.label: Three Separate Buffering Zones of Phosphoric Acid (H₃PO₄)
items.text: Phosphoric acid is triprotic with widely spaced pKa values (~2.1, ~7.2, ~12.4); it buffers ONLY within ±1 pH unit of each individual pKa (NOT uniformly across pH 2–12!). At pH 7.4, H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻ predominate.

items.label: Why ATP Hydrolysis Is Highly Exergonic (ΔG°′ ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol)
items.text: 1) Relieves electrostatic repulsion among 4 clustered negative charges on α/β/γ phosphates; 2) Inorganic phosphate (P_i) and ADP have superior resonance stabilization (less competing oxygen sharing); 3) Greater solvation & entropy.

items.label: Kinetic Stability of DNA/RNA Phosphodiester Backbones
items.text: At pH 7.4, every phosphodiester linkage carries a −1 charge (RO–PO₂⁻–OR′), which electrostatically repels nucleophilic attack by water/hydroxide (RNA hydrolyzes faster in base only because its 2′-OH acts as an internal nucleophile!).

comparison: Negative charge repels OH⁻ hydrolysis & keeps DNA inside cell

figure.caption: Phosphoric acid and a phosphate ester: formal Lewis representations, not localized-bonding measurements.

cue.title: ATP α / β / γ Phosphate Attack & RNA vs. DNA Alkaline Stability
cue.prompt: What phosphoryl transfer or nucleic acid question is asked?

items.label: Kinase Phosphoryl Transfer vs. Synthetase Adenylation
items.outcome: Kinase Attacks γ-P (Releases ADP); Adenylation Attacks α-P (Releases PP_i → 2 P_i)!
items.text: Attacking α-P releases pyrophosphate (PP_i), which inorganic pyrophosphatase immediately hydrolyzes to 2 P_i—providing a double thermodynamic boost!

items.label: Why Does RNA Hydrolyze in Base (NaOH) While DNA Survives?
items.outcome: RNA Has a 2′-OH Group (DNA Is 2′-Deoxy!)
items.text: Base deprotonates the ribose 2′-OH into a 2′-alkoxide right next door, which attacks the phosphorus to form a 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate and cleave the RNA chain!

items.label: Pentavalent Trigonal Bipyramidal Transition State (SN2-Like at P)
items.outcome: In-Line Attack by Nucleophile Opposite the Leaving Group (with Mg²⁺)
items.text: Mg²⁺ chelates the negatively charged phosphate oxygens, neutralizing charge repulsion and polarizing P=O for nucleophilic attack.

trap.title: Calling ATP Bonds "High-Energy Because Breaking Bonds Releases Energy"

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Saying "breaking the P–O bond in ATP releases energy" or claiming phosphate buffers uniformly from pH 2 to pH 12.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Breaking ANY chemical bond is endothermic (requires energy)! ATP hydrolysis releases free energy because the products (ADP + P_i) form stronger bonds, have less charge repulsion, and enjoy greater resonance/solvation than ATP!

app.title: DNA Polymerase 3′-OH Attack on α-Phosphate & Kinase Signaling Cascades

items.label: DNA / RNA Polymerization Direction (5′ → 3′)
items.outcome: Primer 3′-OH Attacks the α-Phosphate of Incoming dNTP
items.text: Forms a new 3′→5′ phosphodiester bond and expels β,γ-pyrophosphate (PP_i), whose hydrolysis drives polymerization forward.

items.label: Ser / Thr / Tyr Protein Kinases vs. Phosphatases
items.outcome: Reversible Electrostatic Switch (+0 OH ⇌ −2 OPO₃²⁻)
items.text: Adding a dianionic phosphate group at pH 7.4 creates new salt bridges with Arg/Lys residues, triggering conformational activation or inhibition.

items.label: Intracellular Phosphate Buffer System
items.outcome: pKa2 = 7.2 Matches Cytosolic pH (~7.2)
items.text: With pH ≈ pKa2, [HPO₄²⁻]/[H₂PO₄⁻] ≈ 1.6:1, providing maximum buffering capacity inside cells.
